hero.name: Sanghyeon Shin
hero.lead: A service planner who digs into users until the answer holds, then builds and ships.
hero.summary: I **analyze all 390K rows**, **rebuild a hypothesis from scratch** when interviews break it, and keep **reading user questions daily** after launch. As a Community Manager Intern at LIKELION, I planned and ran the **14th national hackathon end to end: 80 universities, 2,000 participants**.

about.description_1: I'm a service planner who digs into users before building, and keeps fixing in front of them after.
about.description_2: I started in **frontend development**. What I loved most was **zero to one**: an idea becoming a screen, shipping, and watching people use it. When I joined the 13th cohort's staff at LIKELION, my questions shifted from 'how do we build this' to **'who uses it, why, and how does it become a business'**, and that led me into service planning.
about.what_sub: Most of my time goes into understanding users. I define problems in numbers, let hypotheses break against users, and keep fixing after launch.
about.description_3: As a Community Manager Intern at LIKELION (Apr – Aug 2026), I **planned and ran the 14th national hackathon end to end**: 80 universities, 2,000 participants. I structured the guide in the order participants live it, set the judging policy and platform specs with the team, and ran three warm-up sessions. I **read all 229 questions** that came in over a month and patched the material daily starting from the ones with no answer, and mapped **submission items 1:1 to judging criteria** so teams could predict how they'd be scored. The moment results went public in front of 2,000 people ran on **a console I built**.
about.closing: I want to keep asking what experience people will have with a service, and what one thing will set it apart.
about.training: SSAFY 15th cohort, Non-CS Java track, completed (Jan – Apr 2026)
about.description_4: I've planned 15+ services and built and shipped several of them myself. On FlowPay I interviewed working accountants and **cut anonymous corporate-card reconciliation from 8 steps to 3**, placing 5th of 102 teams. On Y:Wave I **analyzed all 390K Gyeonggi merchant records** and moved the map-first screen to a recommendation list. SonGeul started from **something seniors already do**: writing account numbers by hand. RumiClean, a 3-person client project, is deployed and I'm still revising its user screens and policies.

principles.heading: How I work.

items.t:
Define problems in numbers.
Let hypotheses break against users.
items.d: 562 repos, 53% in a survey, a 41.6%p usage gap. Every plan starts from a number that can be checked. Y:Wave's assumption broke against 390K records and FlowPay's first hypothesis broke in accountant interviews; each time I redefined the problem from scratch.

evidence.t: SonGeul · from what seniors already do

items.t:
Don't leave it in the spec.
Build it and check.
items.d: Where interests collide I set the rule: a 100-point rubric, graded violation verdicts. Then I build the tools and screens myself. Discussion moves faster in front of something that works, and a screen persuades better than a document.

Launch is where user data starts, not where the work ends. Unanswered FAQ-bot questions were collected daily to patch the material; RumiClean's broken pages after deploy were fixed by moving static files to a CDN. Missing tools get built with AI and shipped.
